A professor invites me to his “Black Lit” class; they’re reading Larson’s Passing. One of the black students says, “Sometimes light-skinned blacks think they can fool other blacks, but I can always tell,” looking right through me. After I tell them I am black, I ask the class, “Was I passing when I was just sitting here, before I told you?” A white woman shakes her head desperately, as if I had deliberately deceived her. She keeps examining my face, then turning away as if she hopes I’ll disappear. Why presume “passing” is based on what I leave out and not what she fills in? My father wouldn’t pass, but he might use silence to trap a devil. When he didn’t speak, the man would look up at my father’s face. “What did he write?” my father quizzed me.

Here is a polished version of your text:

A professor once invited me to speak with his "Black Lit" class; they were reading Larsen's *Passing*. One of the Black students remarked, "Sometimes light-skinned Blacks think they can fool other Blacks, but I can always tell"—looking directly through me as she said it. My father, who could easily pass for white, once told me a story: each year, when he went to renew his driver's license, the clerk at the window would fill out the form and ask, without looking up, pencil poised, "White or Black?" My father never claimed to pass—but he might let silence lay a trap for the devil. When he said nothing, the clerk would finally lift his eyes to my father's face. "What do you think he wrote?" my father would ask me, testing.

# On Passing, Perception, and the Politics of Racial Assumption

I was once invited to speak to a "Black Lit" class that was in the midst of discussing Nella Larsen's *Passing*, a novel that explores the fraught territory of racial identity and the choices—conscious or otherwise—that people make about how they are perceived. As someone who is light-skinned, I entered the classroom as something of a living case study, though the students did not yet know it. During the discussion, one black student, unaware of my own racial identity, made a comment suggesting that I might be trying to "fool" the class about who I was—that my presence itself was a kind of performance, an attempt to pass unnoticed or unquestioned among them.

When I revealed that I am, in fact, Black, the moment shifted. I used this revelation as an opportunity to turn the question back on the class itself. I asked them: was I "passing" simply by sitting there silently before disclosing my racial identity? Had I done anything to construct a false impression, or had they simply arrived at their own conclusions based on my appearance alone? The question was not rhetorical for effect—it was meant to expose the mechanics of assumption that undergird our very understanding of what "passing" means.

The response in the room was telling. A white woman in the class grew visibly uncomfortable, her eyes repeatedly searching my face and then darting away, as though she were trying to solve a puzzle or correct some internal miscalculation. Her reaction laid bare something crucial: the perception of "passing" often has less to do with active deception and more to do with the assumptions observers bring into a room. She was not looking for evidence that I had lied; she was recalibrating her own snap judgment, one she had made instantly and without my input.

This raises a deeper question that I posed to the class and continue to pose more broadly: why is "passing" so often framed as an act of deception committed by the individual, rather than as a projection or assumption made by the perceiver? The language we use around passing tends to place the burden of dishonesty on the person whose identity is in question, when in truth, much of what we call "passing" is simply other people filling in gaps with their own biases and expectations. If someone assumes I am white because of my skin tone, and I have said nothing to confirm or deny that assumption, who, precisely, is doing the passing—me, or them?

This dynamic reminds me of my own father, who could pass as white and who once encountered this very question in a strikingly literal way. When applying for his driver's license, he was asked to declare his race. Rather than answering directly, he remained silent, offering no verbal confirmation one way or the other. His silence was not passive; it was a quiet, deliberate act of resistance. By refusing to name his race, he forced the clerk to make the racial determination unaided, based solely on appearance. In doing so, my father shifted the burden of racial categorization away from himself and onto the very system and individual attempting to impose it. He did not lie. He did not claim to be something he was not. He simply declined to participate in a system that demanded he narrate his own identity for the convenience of official record-keeping.

Both of these moments—the classroom exchange and my father's encounter at the DMV—illuminate the same underlying truth: passing is rarely just about the person who is (or isn't) passing. It is, more often, about the assumptions, discomforts, and unexamined biases of those doing the perceiving. The real question is not whether someone chooses to reveal or conceal their racial identity, but why we are so quick to assign motive and deception to silence, when silence itself may simply be a refusal to do the interpretive work that others are unwilling to do themselves.
outputs.L4:
# On Being Read

I am sitting in the back row of a "Black Lit" seminar, my laptop open to a blank document, when the professor asks the class what Nella Larson meant by the title *Passing*. Hands go up. Someone says it's about deception—Clare Kendry lying to her husband, to society, to herself. Someone else says it's about survival, about the impossible choices Black women faced in the 1920s. I nod along, saying nothing, aware that my own face is doing something in this room that none of the pages we've read can quite account for.

I am light-skinned. Black, unambiguously, in my own understanding of myself, in my family's history, in the stories that raised me. But in rooms like this one, my body becomes a kind of Rorschach test. I watch people's eyes flick toward me during the discussion, then away, then back, as if trying to solve for an unknown variable. *Is she one of us, in this conversation? Is she an outside observer? Is she the very phenomenon we're describing?*

The professor, to her credit, catches the current running beneath the room and asks me directly: "What do you think passing means?"

I think of my father.

He used to tell this story about going to the DMV sometime in the late 1970s, back when the forms still had a line for race and the clerks were the ones who filled it in, not the applicants. He was in his twenties then, and the clerk—a white woman with reading glasses pushed low on her nose—looked up at him, looked back down at her form, and wrote "White" without asking him a single question. My father, laughing when he told this story decades later, said he almost corrected her. Almost said, *actually, I'm Black.* But something in him paused. Not shame, he insisted. Not a desire to disappear. Just curiosity, maybe, about what would happen if he let the moment stand. He signed where he needed to sign. He walked out with a license that categorized him in a way he had never categorized himself.

He told me this story not as a confession but as an anecdote, something almost funny, evidence of the absurdity of a system that thought it could sort human beings by looking hard enough at their faces. But the more I turn it over, the less funny it becomes and the more it feels like a key to something.

Because here is what strikes me, sitting in this classroom, watching my classmates try to place me: my father did not pass. He did not construct an elaborate white identity, did not marry into whiteness, did not cut himself off from his family or his history the way Clare Kendry does in Larson's novel. He simply stood still while a stranger's gaze did the work of assigning him a category. The passing—if we can even call it that—happened entirely outside of him. It happened in the clerk's eyes, her assumptions, her need to resolve ambiguity into a single checked box.

This, I tell the class, might be the thing we're missing when we talk about *Passing* purely as a story of active deception. Yes, Clare performs. Yes, she lies by omission, marries a racist man, attends parties where she must monitor every gesture. But underneath all of that performance is a prior act that isn't really an act at all: the initial assumption, made by someone else, that her body means one thing rather than another. Passing requires a passer, sure—but it also requires, maybe even primarily requires, a perceiver. Someone has to look at an ambiguous body and decide, often instantly, often without asking a single question, what that body is.

I think about how often this happens to me outside of any narrative I construct. Cashiers who address me in Spanish. Strangers who compliment my "exotic" look without knowing what they're naming. Black folks who, in the same week, either embrace me instantly as kin or ask, not unkindly, "Wait, are you mixed?" as if my answer will finally settle something for them. In none of these moments am I passing in the way we imagine Clare passing—scheming, calculating, constructing a false self brick by brick. I am simply existing, and other people are doing the sorting, filling the ambiguity of my face with whatever categories feel most legible to them.

Someone in the seminar pushes back gently: doesn't passing require some complicity, some choice to let the misreading stand? And yes—my father chose not to correct the clerk. I sometimes choose not to correct assumptions myself, letting a moment pass rather than launching into a genealogy no stranger actually wants. But complicity is not the same as authorship. The frame was built before we ever stepped into it. The clerk had already decided what she was looking at before my father opened his mouth. My silence, his silence, is not the architecture of the lie—it's just a failure to demolish a house someone else built in seconds, out of habit, out of the deep cultural muscle memory of a country that has always needed to sort bodies into boxes in order to make sense of them.

This, I think, is the real inheritance of *Passing*—not just as a novel but as a word, a concept, a lived condition. We talk about it as though it describes something the ambiguous person *does*. But so often it describes something the ambiguous person merely *allows*, having had no hand in the initial misreading at all. The gaze arrives first. It arrives loaded with history, with the DMV forms of the 1970s, with the "one-drop" logics that still somehow coexist with the visual triage of "you don't look Black enough" or "you don't look white enough" or "what are you, exactly?" The gaze does its sorting work in a fraction of a second, and only afterward does the question of complicity even arise.

By the end of class, we haven't resolved anything—we rarely do, in seminars like this—but something has shifted in how the room understands the text, and maybe in how it understands me. Someone asks if I'd be willing to share my father's DMV story again, in more detail, and I do, watching them listen the way you listen to a joke that turns out, upon reflection, not to be a joke at all.

I walk out into the hallway afterward thinking about how many times a day, invisible to me, someone somewhere is quietly filling in a box on my behalf. Not asking me. Not needing to ask me. Because passing, in the end, may have less to do with what we hide and more to do with what other people, glancing at us for half a second, decide they already know.

# The Language of Contrast: Black, Lit, Larson

In the realm of literature and visual arts, few combinations evoke as much depth as the interplay between darkness and illumination. The word "black" carries profound weight—representing mystery, elegance, sophistication, and sometimes sorrow. It is the color of ink on a page, the shadows that give shape to light, and the void from which stories often emerge.

When something is "lit," it transforms. Light brings clarity, hope, and revelation. In storytelling, moments of illumination often mark turning points—when characters gain understanding or when hidden truths come to the surface. The contrast between black and lit spaces creates visual and emotional tension that artists and writers have explored for centuries.

Larson, as a name, resonates through various creative fields. Jonathan Larson, the composer behind the groundbreaking musical "Rent," used light and darkness metaphorically throughout his work—exploring themes of life, death, and connection in the shadow of the AIDS epidemic. His storytelling illuminated struggles that society often kept in darkness, bringing marginalized voices into the light.

Gary Larson, creator of "The Far Side," used stark black-and-white illustrations to craft humor that illuminated the absurdities of everyday life. His minimalist style proved that simplicity in black ink could spark complex thoughts and laughter.

Together, these elements—black as a canvas, light as revelation, and the creative vision of individuals like Larson—remind us that contrast is essential to meaning. Whether in music, illustration, or literature, the dance between darkness and illumination continues to shape how we understand and express the human experience.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short lyric essay about visiting a "Black Lit" class discussion of Nella Larsen's *Passing* and being mistaken for white.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Being Mistaken

The classroom smelled like coffee and old radiators, twenty desks arranged in the loose circle that signals discussion, not lecture. I came to sit in on Black Lit, guest and witness, folder of notes about Larsen's careful sentences, her scalpel-precise attention to what it costs to be seen.

*Passing* was the week's text. Clare Kendry, dangerous and luminous, moving through Chicago in her white skin like a woman walking a tightrope over her own life. Irene watching her, wanting her, fearing her—the novel a hall of mirrors where everyone is performing something, and the performance might kill you.

The professor asked: *what does it mean to pass, and who gets to choose it?*

I raised my hand to say something about Larsen's irony, the way she never lets you settle into judgment. A student two seats over turned, genuinely curious, and asked me what it was like—*being able to pass*, she said, *if you wanted to.*

The room didn't go silent. It kept breathing, kept being a room. But something in me stood very still.

I am Black. I have always been Black, in every mirror, every family photograph, every line of my own history. But my face, apparently, had performed something else in that moment—had passed without my permission, without my knowledge, become a text she was reading correctly according to its surface and incorrectly according to everything underneath.

I said, *I'm not white.* Simple as that. The way Clare might have said it, if Clare ever told the truth.

The student nodded, embarrassed, and the discussion moved on to Irene's suspicion, her jealousy, the tea cup she does or doesn't drop. But I sat there holding my own strange residue, thinking about how Larsen wrote a novel about the danger of being misread, and I had just been misread inside it, by someone reading it closely, in real time, in a room full of people who would have said—who *did* say, after, apologetically—*we know you're Black, we just meant*—

meant what. Meant that reading is not the same as knowing. Meant that a face is a door that swings open according to the hand that pushes it. Meant that Clare's whole tragedy was that she got to choose only until she didn't, only until someone else's eyes decided the story for her.

I have not passed. I have only, for one classroom minute, been *read* as passing, which is a different violence, smaller and stranger—the violence of being made into the very thing you came to study from the outside.

I stayed for the rest of the discussion. I said my piece about Larsen's irony. But some part of me kept circling that moment, turning it over: how the space between *being* and *being seen* is where the whole novel lives, and how I had just fallen, briefly, into that gap, and had to climb back out using only my own voice, my own insistence, the small flat fact of my *no.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a personal narrative piece exploring racial passing, mixing a classroom scene with a memory about my father and his driver's license?
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Card Couldn't Say

Mrs. Delacroix wrote the word on the board in her careful cursive: **PASSING**. She underlined it twice, like the act itself needed emphasis, needed proof that it had happened at all.

"It's when someone crosses a racial line," she said, "and lives on the other side of it. Sometimes for a day. Sometimes for a lifetime."

I was sixteen and sitting in the third row, and I thought of my father's license.

He kept it in a brown leather wallet that smelled like cedar and Old Spice, and when I was nine or ten I found it while looking for lunch money. There was a box on the license, small and bureaucratic, that asked for race. Someone at the DMV, decades ago, had checked **WHITE**.

My father was not white. My father was the color of strong tea, the color of my own hands, the color that made strangers sometimes ask "what are you" like I was a riddle they'd get extra credit for solving. But there it was in official ink, a government's small lie or his own.

I asked him about it once, at the kitchen table, the license between us like evidence.

"That's just how it was," he said. "Growing up where I grew up." He didn't look up from his coffee. "Sometimes it was safer to let people assume."

*Assume.* Such a soft word for such a hard thing. I didn't understand yet how a box on a form could be a door—one you walked through not because you wanted the room on the other side, but because the room you were in might get you killed, or fired, or refused service at a lunch counter in some town whose name he never told me.

Back in class, Mrs. Delacroix was talking about the historical phenomenon—novels, films, the tragic mulatto trope, Nella Larsen's *Passing*, published in 1929. She talked about it like an artifact, something pressed between the pages of history, dried and flattened and safe to examine.

I raised my hand. I don't know what I meant to say. Maybe: *this isn't only history.* Maybe: *my father did this.* Maybe: *I don't know what to do with the fact that he had to.*

What came out was smaller. "Did people ever pass by accident? Like, did anyone else decide for them?"

She considered this. "Sometimes a clerk would just assume," she said. "Sometimes the assumption became the record."

*The assumption became the record.* I thought about that phrase for years afterward. How my father's face, his own particular brown, had been looked at by someone behind a counter and translated into a single letter that didn't fit. How he had let it stand. How the not-correcting was its own kind of quiet, its own survival math: *what do I gain by arguing, what do I lose by staying silent, which door do I walk through today.*

He passed—not in the grand, decades-long, life-altering way of the old stories, not building a whole new self on the other side of the color line. Just small, incremental passings. A license that lied so his life could go on unbothered a little more easily. A softening of his features when he spoke a certain way to certain people, a slight vise in his voice.

I never had that option, not exactly. My skin reads different, reads unambiguous, or maybe I just never learned my father's particular grammar of survival. But I think about that word he used—*safer*—and I understand now that it was never about desire. Nobody wants to disappear from themselves. They want to still be standing at the end of the day.

The bell rang. Mrs. Delacroix erased **PASSING** from the board, the word disintegrating into chalk dust, into history, into whatever bin we file uncomfortable inheritances into.

I still have that wallet. The license expired decades ago, laminate peeling at the corner, my father's young face gazing out from under that small, wrong word. I don't correct it. I don't know if correcting it would even mean anything now.

Some doors, once you've walked through them, you carry on your back forever, a shape only you and the people who love you can see.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a reflective, literary vignette in first person about being light-skinned and Black, incorporating a moment from reading Larsen's *Passing* in a college class.
counterfactuals.output:
The professor's copy of *Passing* was so worn the spine had given up entirely, pages loose as teeth in an old man's mouth, and I remember thinking that seemed right somehow—that a book about the instability of identity should itself be falling apart at the seams.

We were discussing Clare Kendry, the way she moves through the world like water finding its level, and Professor Alvarez asked the room what it meant to "pass," whether it was betrayal or survival or something with no clean name at all. I sat there with my coffee going cold, watching the discussion unspool around me, and felt the particular loneliness of being a case study in a room full of theories.

I am light enough that strangers have often paused before speaking to me, doing some private arithmetic behind their eyes. I have been asked, more times than I can count, *what are you*, as though I were a math problem instead of a person, as though my face were an equation waiting to be solved. Growing up, my grandmother would look at photographs of her mother—skin like coffee with cream, hair pressed straight for church—and say, *she could have gone, you know, if she'd wanted to*. As though passing were a door always slightly ajar, a temptation requiring vigilance to resist. As though whiteness were water and we were all just trying not to drown, or trying not to swim toward it, I was never sure which.

In class, someone raised their hand and said Clare's death at the end felt like punishment, like the novel couldn't let her get away with it. Another student disagreed—said it was more like release, like she'd been living a held breath for years and something had to give. I didn't say anything. I was thinking about my own face, how it has never quite settled into legibility for other people, how I have watched them search it the way you search a word you can almost remember, waiting for it to resolve into something they recognize.

What Larsen understood, I think, is that passing was never really about fooling anyone. It was about the exhaustion of being seen wrong, or seen too much, or seen as a threshold instead of a person. Clare wasn't hiding so much as she was tired—tired of translation, tired of being asked to explain herself in a language that was never built to hold her.

I closed the book that night and looked at my own hands, unable to certify anything, and understood that this—the not-quite, the both-and, the door that opens onto more doors—was not a puzzle I would solve so much as a life I would simply have to keep living, one ambiguous, unresolved day at a time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a prose poem or memoir excerpt that questions who gets to define "passing," using both a classroom anecdote and a family story about race and bureaucracy.
counterfactuals.output:
# On Passing

The county clerk's office in 1962 had a particular smell—mimeograph ink and radiator dust—and my grandmother stood at the counter for forty minutes while a man decided what she was. This is the story my mother tells at Thanksgiving, the way some families tell stories about wars: my grandmother's papers said one thing, her skin said another to the man behind the counter, and somewhere in that gap he made a decision that would follow her for the rest of her life. He looked at her the way you'd check a fruit for bruising. He wrote down a word that wasn't the word she'd said. She didn't argue. You didn't, then. The bureaucracy of race has always required someone to be the arbiter, some tired man with a rubber stamp deciding where the borders of a body should fall.

I think about this in Mrs. Halloway's tenth-grade classroom, decades later, different kind of counter. We're discussing *The Bluest Eye* and a boy near the window says some people just don't act like their race, and the room does that thing where twenty people simultaneously look at their desks. I still don't know what my face did. I know I said nothing, which is its own kind of answer. I know that "acting like your race" is a sentence that assumes race has a script, a costume, a walk, and that somewhere there's a stage manager checking you against the character notes. Pass or fail. Convincing or not.

My grandmother was told what she was by a man with a form to fill out. I was told what I wasn't by a boy with a hall pass in his pocket. Both of them believed they were simply observing a fact, the way you'd note that water is wet. Neither of them understood that they were the fact—that "passing" only exists because someone built a checkpoint and put themselves in charge of it. The border guard doesn't discover the border. He invents it every time he asks for papers.

I want to tell you my grandmother "passed" for something, but that word implies a performance, a successful fraud, when what actually happened is that a stranger's assumptions became a government record. I want to tell you I corrected that boy in class, but what actually happened is that his sentence became a small brick in a wall I'd spend years learning to see, let alone dismantle.

What I know now: the counter is not neutral. The classroom is not neutral. Every space where someone gets to say *you are this and not that* carries the residue of every clerk's office, every hallway, every moment when a category became more real than a person standing in front of it, waiting, the way my grandmother waited, for someone else to decide who she'd been all along.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a creative nonfiction piece where the narrator, visiting a literature class discussing *Passing*, reflects on identity, perception, and a childhood story their father told them.
counterfactuals.output:
# What Passes Between Us

The classroom smells like coffee and radiator dust. I am sitting in the back, a visitor, watching twenty-two-year-olds underline passages in Nella Larsen's *Passing* with the fierce concentration of people who suspect the answer to the quiz will be somewhere in the margins.

The professor asks: "What does it cost Clare to pass?"

A student says everything. Another says nothing, because passing is a kind of theft—you take what was never offered.

I write nothing in my own notebook. I am thinking of my father, who is not in this book, who has never read this book, who would not know what to do with a novel where the tragedy is a woman falling from a window and no one can say for certain if she jumped or was pushed or simply forgot, for one dangerous second, which room she was standing in.

---

My father told me a story when I was young enough to still ask *is this true* about everything.

He said: when he came to this country, an official at a desk misheard his name and wrote down another one. Not close. Not a cousin-name. A whole different animal of a name, English in its bones. My father did not correct him.

*Why not,* I asked, the way children ask why not about everything, expecting an answer with a door in it.

*Because,* he said, *the man behind the desk had already decided who I was before I opened my mouth. I only chose which version of that decision to survive.*

I did not understand this as a child. I understood it as an adult, sitting in the back of a classroom that is not mine, listening to strangers discuss Clare Kendry's face like it is a locked box someone finally forced open.

---

Larsen writes that Clare has "ivory skin" and "creamy" this and "golden" that—the language of desserts, of things meant to be consumed by someone else's mouth. The student in the front row says *she's basically performing whiteness as a survival mechanism* and I think: yes, but also no, also it is more complicated than performance, because a performance implies there is a true self waiting in the wings, changed out of costume, ready to go home.

What if there is no home. What if the costume is the only body you've got.

My father wore his new name like a coat he never quite broke in. It fit him at the shoulders but not the wrists. I watched him sign it on forms his whole life, watched the pen hesitate for one-tenth of a second before each signature, a hitch so small only a daughter watching too closely would notice it. That hitch was the truest thing about him. That hitch was him, still standing in the doorway of the old name, one foot in each room.

---

Irene Redfield spends the novel terrified of what Clare might cost her—not just the marriage, not just the safety, but the unbearable mirror of her. Because to see someone pass is to be reminded that identity was never solid ground to begin with. It was always this: a series of rooms, and someone else standing at the door deciding what you're allowed to carry through it.

The professor asks if Clare's fall was suicide.

The class argues. I do not raise my hand, but if I did, I would say: it doesn't matter. What matters is that a woman spent her whole life being looked at and reinterpreted by other people's eyes, and one day the window was open, and the ground was very far down, and perhaps for a moment she forgot to hold on—not because she wanted to die, but because she had spent so many years managing what people saw that she forgot, briefly, that she was also a body, subject to gravity, unmanaged and unmanageable, falling exactly the way any falling thing falls.

---

After class, I walk outside into weather that does not care what name I go by. I think about my father, now an old man, who still hitches for that tenth of a second before he signs.

I do not think passing is only about race, though the book is precise about that violence and I don't want to blur its edges into something softer than it is. But I think passing is also this: the specific loneliness of being seen as a costume by people who never ask what's underneath, and eventually forgetting to ask yourself.

My father chose a name to survive a desk, a decision, a door already closing. I have spent my life trying to learn which of my own names are costumes and which are simply—finally—mine. Some days I can't tell the difference. Some days I think that not being able to tell is the whole American inheritance, passed to me like a coat with sleeves too long, hemmed by hands I never met, tailored for a body they imagined instead of the one that showed up.

The novel ends with a body on the ground and a question no one can answer.

I walk to my car thinking: some of us live our whole lives in that same unanswerable second—between the window and the pavement, between the name we were given and the one we chose, between the room we started in and the one we're still, always, falling toward.
